machineListenFindings.pronunciationText: Last video ended on a count that doubles every hour, two to the x. Money can double too, just more slowly. Put a thousand dollars into a savings account that doubles every ten years. Count in thousands of dollars and in decades, and the balance is two to the x. Here it is beside e to the x. Both start at a height of one. E to the x leaves that point with a slope of exactly one, because it's its own derivative. But two to the x is flatter there. So the derivative of two to the x can't just be two to the x. Then how fast is the balance really growing? Here's the strange part. The answer contains a logarithm. Why would a log turn up when you differentiate an exponential?

Now let's prove it for any positive base ay. The natural log of ay is the power that turns e into ay, so ay equals e to the natural log of ay. So ay to the x is e raised to a new power, x times the natural log of ay. Call that power u. The base is fixed, so the natural log of ay is just ay number, and d u by d x is the natural log of ay. And d y by d u is e to the u. The chain rule multiplies them. Put the power back, and that e to the u is ay to the x again. So the derivative of ay to the x is the natural log of ay, times ay to the x. Try ay equals e. The natural log of e is one, so you get e to the x back, the rule you already know.

What if the base is less than two? Slide it down. At ay equals one, the curve flattens into the line y equals one, with gradient zero. The rule agrees, because the natural log of one is zero. Keep going to a half. Now the curve falls. The natural log of a half is minus point six nine three, so the gradient is negative, while the height stays positive. A half to the x is two to the minus x, the mirror image of two to the x. And the base must be positive. The natural log of ay negative number doesn't exist, and a negative base can't be raised to every power.

Find the gradient of y equals two to the x at x equals three. Here the base is two. Copy two to the x, then multiply by the natural log of two. So d y by d x is the natural log of two, times two to the x. At x equals three, two cubed is eight, so the gradient is eight times the natural log of two, about five point five five. For the account, that's eight thousand dollars after thirty years, growing at about five and a half thousand dollars a decade. On the graph, the height is eight, and the gradient is point six nine three times that. If you wrote just two to the x, you'd get eight. That's the slope e to the x has at that height.
